utterances.text: Patient: Ahh, yes doctor — I had TB 2-3 years back, took full course of medicines. And blood transfusion was given after my second delivery, some heavy bleeding had happened.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Understood. Do you cycle or do any physical activity regularly? And do you smoke or take liquor?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Doctor, I do some cycling every day in the morning, only small rounds. Liquor I take after meals sometimes, my husband also does. But I am not a chain smoker — I confirmed to my husband also, I have never touched cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Good. Now, are you living in a city area or rural area? Any pets at home or smoke exposure from kitchen or surroundings?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: We are originally from rural area doctor, shifted here three years back. We have pets — two cats at home. And earlier in village there was always cooking smoke, wood fire only we were using.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Any itching or rash on the scalp or skin? Any breathlessness on climbing stairs?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: There is some itching on my scalp over a year, I thought it is just dryness. And yes doctor, breathlessness comes when I climb to the second floor.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Have you done any heart test before — like an Echo or ECG? Any medicines you are currently taking?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Umm, ECG was done at the camp but Echo — I doubt it doctor, I don't think I ever did that one. For anxiety they had given some tablet — I think it was lorazepam — but I stopped on my own.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Based on everything — the palpitations, mild chest pain, elevated BP, and breathlessness — this looks like hypertension with possible early cardiac involvement. The anxiety is also contributing to her palpitations.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: I am prescribing atenolol for the BP and palpitations — take it every day in the morning. For anxiety, I am giving a very small dose of lorazepam, only when symptoms are bad, not regularly.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Doctor, this atenolol — will it cause any side effects? I have heard dizziness comes.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Some patients do get dizziness initially, especially if you get up too fast. Also, the liquor you take after meals — please stop that completely, it pushes the BP up further and reacts badly with atenolol.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Continue your cycling — that is good. But we must do an Echo and a lipid profile to check the heart properly. Also a chest X-ray given the old TB history.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Doctor, the itching on my scalp — should I be worried? And the pets at home, should I remove them?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: The scalp itching may be related to the pets or just dryness — let us do a skin allergy test to be sure. You don't need to remove them immediately, but keep the scalp clean and we will review after results.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Good morning, please have a seat. How are you feeling after the discharge?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Doctor, honestly not much better. The itching is still there and the rash in the umbilical region looks worse to me. Why was I even discharged so early?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: I understand your concern. Can you describe the itching — is it throbbing kind of sensation or more like a burn?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: It is more like stabbing and worse at night. During the day when I am busy at my stall it is okay, but at night it drives me crazy.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Is the rash spreading beyond the umbilical region? Any redness or discharge from the area?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: It has spread a little to the abdomen sides also. There is no discharge but the redness is definitely there. And this itching is happening weekly since before my admission also.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Any family member was sick with similar skin rash or fungal infection recently?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Yes, my wife had similar itching last month. And I visit crowded places like the market daily for my work, so how can I even avoid these things?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: That is important information. Do you work night shifts at your food stall? How are your sleep habits?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: I work from afternoon till midnight doctor. My sleep habits are very irregular — I sleep maybe four hours, sometimes less. You are going to tell me to sleep more, right? I cannot afford that.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Poor sleep does reduce immunity and worsen skin infections. Also, do you drink alcohol at all?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: I am an occasional drinker, just socially. And I drink a lot of tea to stay awake at night — around five to six cups. Is that a problem?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Based on your symptoms and examination, this is a case of dermatophyte fungal infection — commonly called ringworm — aggravated by sweating, heat exposure at the food stall, and low immunity from poor sleep.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: But doctor, I had this even before. Why did the hospital not treat it properly the first time? Was there something missed?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: The hospital treated your acute skin flare post-op. This underlying fungal infection was chronic and needs outpatient follow-up treatment. It was not missed — it needs a longer course.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: I am prescribing terbinafine cream to apply twice on the umbilical region and abdomen daily, and fluconazole 150mg tablet once a week for four weeks. Also, cetirizine 10mg at night for the itching.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: That is three medicines! Will the fluconazole not affect my stomach? I have a sensitive system. And can I take it with tea?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Fluconazole can occasionally cause nausea or stomach upset, so take it after food. Excessive tea with cetirizine may reduce its effectiveness — try to reduce to two cups at night.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Also doctor, I am having some pain in the teeth since last week — is that related to all this or separate?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: The tooth pain in the teeth is likely separate — is it throbbing or constant?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: It is throbbing doctor, especially when I drink hot tea. It has been there post-op from my hospital stay, I think stress worsened it.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: For the tooth pain I would advise you to see a dentist separately. Meanwhile do a KOH scraping test and complete blood count today so we can confirm the fungal infection type and check your immunity levels.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: More tests — more money, doctor. Can these not wait? I already spent so much during the admission.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: I understand, but if the KOH scraping test is skipped and you have a different fungal strain, the medicines may not work. Also, your night shift exposure at crowded places and contact with your wife's illness means reinfection risk is high — we must confirm the diagnosis properly.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Alright doctor, fine. I will get it done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Good afternoon, please come in and sit down. How are you feeling today?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Ahh, doctor, I am a little better than before but there is still pain on the right side, especially post-op. It is slightly painful most of the time but becomes unbearable worse at night.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Okay, so you were hospitalised two weeks ago for the hernia repair — the laparoscopy was done, correct? And you also had the piles and abscess treated at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Yeah, doctor, all three were done together. The surgeon said the intestine repair went well but the abscess area is still giving me trouble.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Is there any bleeding or discharge from the wound site still? And any fever?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Umm, discharge is there once a day when I clean the wound. Fever is almost never now, doctor, only very mild in evenings sometimes.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Now I need to ask — I see in your file you were on rosuvastatin for cholesterol. Are you still taking it or did you change something on your own?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Ahh, doctor, I stopped the rosuvastatin on my own after surgery because my neighbour said it would interfere with healing. I also started taking antihistamines for the itching on the wound without telling anyone.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: You should never stop rosuvastatin without my advice — this can cause your cholesterol to spike suddenly. And self-medicating with antihistamines is risky especially when you are also on spironolactone for your fluid retention. These can interact badly.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: I did not know that, doctor. I am also on spironolactone for the swelling in my legs that was there before hospitalisation. I thought it was okay to continue it.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Your history mentions rheumatoid arthritis and anxiety disorder. Are those being managed separately? Any joint pain flare-up post-op?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: The rheumatoid arthritis is controlled doctor, I doubt it caused any flare this time. The anxiety disorder is a bit worse since the surgery but I am managing.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: You work in a mine, is that right? Tell me about your occupational exposures — any contact with crowded places, chemicals, or heavy dust underground?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Yes doctor, I work in the mine office but I do go underground sometimes. There is lot of dust and we are always in crowded places during shift changes. I have been doing this for 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: That is a long time. Any episodes of malaria or anemia in the past given the exposure in that environment?

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Doctor, I had malaria once about three years back. And they told me I have mild anemia — it was detected at the time of my pre-surgery blood work two weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: What about your diet and physical activity? Are you non-vegetarian? That matters for your recovery from anemia.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Yes doctor, I am non-vegetarian, so I eat chicken and eggs regularly. But physical activity I have quit completely after the surgery because of the pain on the right side.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Based on everything, you have post-operative wound infection at the abscess site, anemia that needs correction, and your intestine repair looks adequate but we need to monitor. The swelling in your legs may be related to fluid retention partly worsened by stopping spironolactone irregularly.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: So what should I do now doctor? I am a bit worried about all these medicines together. Should I restart everything?

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Yes, restart rosuvastatin tonight itself — do not skip it again. Continue spironolactone as originally prescribed. I am stopping the self-started antihistamines and instead prescribing cetirizine which is safer in your current state. For the anemia I am adding ferrous sulphate tablets once a day with food.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: We will do a complete blood count and wound swab culture today to check the infection and anemia levels. Light physical activity like short walks can be restarted carefully — do not strain the right side.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Doctor, should I avoid going back to the mine with all this crowded places and dust? The wound is still open a little.

utterances.speaker: Doctor
utterances.text: Doctor: Absolutely avoid the underground area and crowded places for at least another three to four weeks. Dust exposure can worsen the wound infection and given your history of malaria, crowded damp environments are risky. Wear a mask if you must go to the office level. Come back in one week with the wound swab culture report.

utterances.speaker: Patient
utterances.text: Patient: Thank you so much doctor, I will follow everything you said this time properly.
